---
title: "Methods"
---

This systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024575661) and followed PRISMA reporting guidelines [@chien_effectiveness_2026].

## Search Strategy {#sec-search}

A comprehensive literature search was conducted from database inception to July 22, 2024, in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines using Ovid MEDLINE, Embase.com, Web of Science Core Collection, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, and APA PsycINFO databases.
The search strategy incorporated controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to anxiety, depression, and supplementation with B vitamins, vitamin C, vitamin D, zinc, magnesium, selenium, or iron. A validated filter was applied to identify randomized controlled trials [@royle_making_2007]. The complete search strategy is provided in the Appendix.

All records were de-duplicated using EndNote [@noauthor_endnote_2023] and imported into Covidence Systematic Review Software [@veritas_health_innovation_covidence_nodate] for screening. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were independently reviewed by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer.

## Eligibility Criteria {#sec-eligibility}

RCTs evaluating the effects of vitamin or mineral supplementation on depressive or anxiety symptoms in adults were included. Non-randomized studies, observational studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, case reports and series, animal studies, and non–peer-reviewed publications were excluded. Given feasibility constraints, RCTs not published in English and articles without accessible full text were also excluded.

Eligible participants included adults ≥18 years old from the general population who exhibited clinically significant depressive or anxiety symptoms or met diagnostic criteria for a depressive or anxiety disorder. Anxiety disorders encompassed social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder. Depressive disorders included major depressive disorder, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, persistent depressive disorder, postpartum depression, seasonal affective disorder, dysthymic disorder, and vascular depression. Trials enrolling individuals with bipolar disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, psychotic disorders, schizophrenia, or neurocognitive disorders were excluded.

Eligible interventions included supplementation with B vitamins, vitamin C, vitamin D, zinc, magnesium, selenium, or iron, either alone or in combination. No restrictions were placed on dose, formulation, or duration. Herbal remedies or supplements outside of these prespecified nutrients were excluded. Comparator conditions included placebo, standard care, or no active supplementation.

Eligible trials were required to have a minimum follow-up duration of four weeks, as shorter trials were considered unlikely to capture clinically meaningful changes in depressive or anxiety symptoms. When multiple publications reported on overlapping datasets, the study with the largest sample and most comprehensive outcome data was retained.


## Data Extraction {#sec-data-extraction}
Two reviewers independently extracted data, with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Extracted study characteristics included author, year, country, setting, funding source, recruitment method, randomization procedures, blinding, intervention duration, and assessment timepoints. Participant characteristics included sample size, age, sex distribution, diagnostic criteria, baseline symptom severity, baseline micronutrient status, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and attrition rates. Intervention details included supplement type, dose, formulation, frequency, route of administration, and adherence. Comparator conditions were categorized as placebo, standard care, or no active intervention.
For each study, mean scores and standard deviations for validated depression and anxiety scales at baseline and follow-up were extracted, along with reported changes over time and adverse events. When multiple scales were used within a study, outcomes were preferentially extracted from the most widely validated instrument. When essential data were missing, corresponding authors were contacted for clarification when feasible.

## Risk of Bias Assessment {#sec-risk-bias}

Methodological quality was assessed independently by two reviewers using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 1 (RoB 1) tool for randomized controlled trials, which was the tool available in Covidence at the time of review [@higgins_cochrane_2011; @sterne_rob_2019]. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer consulted when necessary. Studies were evaluated across the seven standard RoB 1 domains and categorized as having low, unclear, or high risk of bias according to criteria in the Cochrane Handbook. Overall risk of bias for each study reflected the highest level of concern across domains. When information was insufficient, investigators were contacted for clarification; if unavailable, the domain was rated as unclear.

## Outcome Measures {#sec-outcomes}

The primary outcome assessed was change in depression or anxiety symptom severity measured with a validated rating scale at the end of the study (e.g., Beck Depression Inventory, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale). Studies that did not report sufficient quantitative outcome data were excluded. Given that different scales were used across trials, outcomes were harmonized using standardized mean differences (SMDs). When multiple scales were reported for the same condition within a study, the most commonly used scale across studies was selected. A complete list of scales and their frequency of use, as well as how outcomes were constructed, is provided in the Appendix. 

Secondary outcomes included pre–post changes in serum micronutrient concentrations and adverse events. For change in serum micronutrients, we expressed differences as mean differences. For adverse events, effect estimates were expressed as odds ratios.

## Statistical Analysis {#sec-stat-analysis}

Analysis was conducted using a Bayesian network meta-analysis that combined direct and indirect comparisons under a hierarchical random-effects model with study-level random effects [@lu_combination_2004]. The primary network meta-analysis was restricted to studies at low overall risk of bias; all other eligible studies—including two low risk of bias studies with interventions comparing doses of the same vitamins—were retained for prespecified sensitivity analyses. Models were fit using the `brms` package in `R`, which implements Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling via `Stan` to estimate posterior distributions of treatment effects [@burkner_advanced_2018; @r_core_team_r_2025; @gabry_cmdstanr_2025]. Additional model details, including priors, number of chains and iterations, convergence diagnostics, and handling of multi-arm trials, are provided in the Appendix.

The assumption of transitivity may be threatened by uneven distributions of baseline vitamin deficiency and baseline depression or anxiety status across interventions. We therefore evaluated transitivity by examining whether key potential effect modifiers were similarly distributed across treatment comparisons. Specifically, we assessed sex distribution, baseline micronutrient deficiency, baseline symptom severity, baseline diagnostic status, and adjunctive antidepressant use, each of which may plausibly influence treatment response. Study- and comparison-level characteristics were visually inspected to identify systematic imbalances across the network. In addition, prespecified network meta-regression models were used to formally evaluate effect modification by these study-level characteristics, and subgroup-specific estimates are reported.

A common between-study heterogeneity parameter (τ) was assumed across interventions within each outcome network. Heterogeneity was interpreted by comparing τ to the scale of observed treatment effects and by examining prediction intervals. Coherence (consistency) was assessed using node-splitting models and a design-by-treatment interaction model [@dias_checking_2010; @dias_evidence_2013]. Residual heterogeneity and inconsistency were further explored using prespecified meta-regression models evaluating potential sources of variability, including risk of bias, baseline symptom severity, baseline micronutrient levels, year and country of study, standard error, and duration of follow-up. Contour-enhanced funnel plots were used to assess potential small-study effects.

When augmentation trials formed a disconnected subnetwork from the main placebo-controlled network, they were modeled separately and did not contribute to indirect comparisons in the primary network.
Certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework, which assesses six domains: within-study bias, reporting bias, indirectness, imprecision, heterogeneity, and incoherence [@nikolakopoulou_cinema_2020]. Confidence ratings were generated for all interventions relative to placebo and for all contrasts present in the network (see the Appendix).
